title: Fools, Loafers, Gossips and Liars
overview: This chapter is a string of sharp, often funny comparisons warning about four kinds of people: the fool, the lazy person, the troublemaker and the smooth liar.

parts.label: Honor does not suit a fool (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: In Israel snow in summer was out of place and rain at harvest could ruin the crop, and honoring a fool is just as wrong; fools need a rod the way a horse needs a whip. A curse spoken against someone who did nothing to deserve it is like a bird that flits past and never lands: it has no power over them.

parts.label: Two ways to answer (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: These opposite sayings sit side by side on purpose. Sometimes you should not stoop to a fool's level, and sometimes you must answer so they do not think they have won; the wisdom lies in knowing which moment you are in.

parts.label: Trusting fools backfires (vv. 6-12)
parts.note: Sending a fool with a message, or letting one quote wise sayings, is as useless as a lame leg and as risky as a thorn in a drunk's hand. Verse 10 is very hard to translate and scholars are unsure of its exact meaning, but verse 12 makes a clear final point: someone who thinks they already know it all is even harder to help than a fool.

parts.label: The lazy person's excuses (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: With gentle mockery, the lazy person invents a lion in the street to avoid going out, rolls over in bed like a door swinging on its hinge, and cannot even lift food to their mouth. The sharpest jab is that they are sure they are smarter than everyone else.

parts.label: Meddling, deceit and gossip (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: Jumping into someone else's fight is like grabbing a stray dog by the ears, and deceiving a neighbor and then claiming it was only a joke is like a madman shooting flaming, deadly arrows. Gossip feeds quarrels the way wood feeds a fire, and people swallow it eagerly like tasty treats.

parts.label: Charming words, hidden hatred (vv. 23-28)
parts.note: Warm words over an evil heart are like a clay pot coated with silver dross, the cheap leftover from refining silver that only looks precious (some scholars read the image as a shiny glaze instead), and seven abominations simply means a heart full of evil. Such deceit tends to come out in public eventually, and people who set traps for others often fall into them themselves.

think: When someone says something foolish or hostile to you, how do you decide whether it is worth answering at all?
